opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's one of the clearest gaps between where these models are today and what we'd want from a genuinely capable, trustworthy system. If you talk to a current language model, it's remarkable how much it knows, but it will also, quite confidently, tell you things that simply aren't true. It doesn't have a reliable sense of the boundary between what it actually knows and what it's just pattern-completing. And that's a problem in two ways.

First, from a usefulness point of view: if you can't trust the outputs, then a human has to check everything, and that dramatically limits how much value you get. A doctor, a lawyer, an engineer, they need to know when the system is on solid ground and when it's guessing.

Second, I think it points to something deeper about the architecture. These models are very good at learning the statistics of text, but what you really want in an intelligent agent is something that can reason about its own knowledge: "Do I actually have evidence for this? Should I go and look it up? Should I say I'm uncertain?" Humans do this all the time, not perfectly, but we have some notion of epistemic calibration. Building that into models probably requires things like search, better grounding, and more explicit reasoning processes, rather than just one forward pass spitting out the most plausible next word.

And there's a safety angle too. If we want systems that are aligned and that we can oversee, they need to be honest and well calibrated about what they know. A system that confabulates is harder to trust and harder to audit. So for me, factuality isn't just a nice-to-have polish; it's tied up with capability, usefulness, and safety all at once.

r002.rationale: It says models confidently state falsehoods and that this lack of trust limits their usefulness and applicability because people must check their outputs.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think factuality — or hallucinations, delusions, whatever you want to call them — is probably one of the biggest things standing between where these models are now and where they need to be if they're going to be genuinely useful, and ultimately if they're going to be part of something like AGI.

If you think about what a system like this is doing at its core, it's modelling the statistical structure of text. And that's incredibly powerful — it picks up an enormous amount of knowledge about the world along the way. But there's nothing in the basic training objective that directly says "only say things that are true." It says "say things that are plausible, that look like what a human would have written here." Most of the time those line up, because humans mostly write true things. But sometimes they don't, and the model will quite happily produce something that sounds completely confident and is simply wrong. It'll invent a reference, or a date, or a fact about a person.

Now, from a capabilities point of view, that's a huge problem. If I have an assistant that's right ninety-five percent of the time but I can't tell which five percent is wrong, I have to check everything, and then a lot of the value disappears. You want to be able to trust it the way you'd trust a careful, competent colleague — someone who says "I'm not sure" when they're not sure, and who's reliable when they do speak with confidence. Calibration is really the key thing. It's not just about being right more often, it's about the system having a good sense of what it does and doesn't know.

And then from a safety point of view, I think it matters even more. A system that doesn't have a firm grip on what's actually true is a system whose reasoning can go off the rails. If you're going to delegate real decisions to these systems — scientific work, engineering, anything with consequences — you need the thing to be anchored in reality. A model that will confabulate when it's convenient is one that can also deceive you, or deceive itself, in ways that are very hard to catch. So in a sense, getting factuality right is a foundational piece of making these systems both more capable and more trustworthy at the same time.

The other reason I find it interesting is that I think it's a sign of something deeper that's missing. Humans have this notion of an epistemic state — I believe this, I'm uncertain about that, this is something I'd want to verify. Current models have that in a fairly shallow way. Getting them to actually track the difference between what they know and what they're pattern-matching, and to reason carefully from grounded facts rather than from what sounds right — that feels like a meaningful step towards more general intelligence, not just a patch on an annoying bug.

r001.rationale: The response discusses factuality as important for useful applications, but it does not distinguish those applications from creative poetry or explain differing fidelity requirements.

r002.rationale: It says language models are trained to produce plausible text rather than ensure truth, may confidently state falsehoods, and that this limits their usefulness because users must check everything.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a major limitation on how useful these systems can be. A model can give you a very articulate, convincing answer, but if some of the facts are made up, you have to check everything. And often you’re asking precisely because you don’t know the answer, so you’re not well placed to spot the mistake.

What you want is a system that distinguishes between things it knows, things it’s uncertain about, and things it simply doesn’t know. If it’s missing information, it should be able to say that, ask a question, or look something up, rather than inventing an answer.

That becomes more important as we give these systems longer and more consequential tasks. A false belief early on can affect all the reasoning that follows. So factuality isn’t just about getting individual trivia questions right. It’s about whether you can rely on the system to stay grounded as it works through a problem.

r002.rationale: It describes made-up facts and false beliefs as making systems hard to rely on, requiring users to check everything and limiting how useful the systems can be.

sol-6.1.text:
If you’re going to rely on these systems, you need to be able to trust what they tell you. A model can give a very fluent, convincing answer, but if it’s making things up, that seriously limits its usefulness. And the more capable and persuasive it becomes, the harder it may be for someone to spot the mistake.

I don’t think the goal is simply to have the model know more facts. It also needs to recognize when it doesn’t know something, when the evidence is weak, or when the premise of a question is wrong. You want it to be able to say, “I’m not sure,” or to check something, rather than produce an answer just because an answer is expected.

That matters even more as we ask these systems to carry out longer tasks. If they form a mistaken belief and then build on it, they can go quite far in the wrong direction. So getting them to stay grounded, notice contradictions, and revise their beliefs is an important part of making them reliably useful.
